# Sourdough Discard Recipes

## Overview

Keeping a starter means pouring off a cup of discard every time I refresh it, and throwing that away always felt wasteful, so I collect it in a jar in the fridge and bake with it through the week. The discard is not dead; it is still full of wild yeast and lactic acid, just hungry, which is why these recipes lean on a fresh feed and a little patience rather than quick shortcuts. My three regulars are thin crackers, overnight pancakes and crumpets, and between them they use up almost everything I pour off. The crackers are the fastest and the most rewarding, since they need nothing but a few store-cupboard ingredients and a hot oven. The pancakes want an overnight sponge so the batter has time to reawaken and turn bubbly. The crumpets are the fussiest of the three because they depend on bicarbonate to open the tight network of holes across the top. Everything here is genuinely unstarted by a fresh feed, meaning the discard goes in straight from the jar, cold and unfed, and the recipe relies on the acid already present to do the work. That one rule keeps the whole chapter simple, and it means you never need to plan these bakes around the starter's schedule.

## Steps

1. For the crackers, weigh 200 g of discard into a bowl, add 40 g of melted butter and a pinch of salt, and mix it into a soft, slightly sticky dough.
2. Roll the dough out as thin as you can manage between two sheets of baking paper, then peel the top sheet away and cut the sheet into rough squares with a knife or a pizza wheel.
3. Slide the paper onto a tray and bake the crackers at 180 C for 25 minutes, turning the tray once, until they are crisp and evenly browned at the edges.
4. For the overnight pancakes, whisk the discard with a little flour and a splash of milk in the evening to make a loose sponge, cover it, and leave it on the counter overnight while the wild yeast comes back to life.
5. In the morning, beat an egg, a tablespoon of melted butter, a teaspoon of sugar and a pinch of salt into the bubbly sponge, then cook ladlefuls in a hot buttered pan until the bubbles burst and the edges set.
6. For the crumpets, warm the discard with a little water and sugar, then stir through flour and let the batter rise until it is visibly active and foamy.
7. Just before cooking, dissolve a quarter of a teaspoon of bicarbonate of soda in a spoonful of warm water and beat it thoroughly into the batter, which loosens it and forces the bubbles to the surface.
8. Cook the crumpets in buttered rings over a low heat until the tops are crowded with little holes and the batter has set, then flip each one for a brief moment to colour the top. Lift them out and wrap them in a clean tea towel so the steam keeps the sides soft while the tops stay crisp.

## Notes

The important thing to understand is that discard straight from the fridge is sour and slow, so the recipes that rise overnight depend on that time to wake the culture back up. Never treat the discard as an inert ingredient, because it is a living mixture and a very old one will taste strongly acidic and can need a pinch of sugar to balance it. The crackers are the most forgiving; if the dough springs back while you roll it, rest it for ten minutes and try again, and if it tears, patch it with a wet finger. Keep them thin, because a thick cracker stays chewy and never crisps through. The pancakes want a thicker batter than a boxed mix gives, so let the sponge dictate how much flour it needs rather than measuring exactly. The crumpets live or die on the bicarbonate, which must go in at the very last moment and be beaten in hard; without it the batter makes flat, solid pucks. Butter the rings well, keep the heat low, and be patient. Any of these freeze well once cooled, and the crackers and crumpets both reheat in a dry pan in a couple of minutes. I keep a small jar of discard going specifically for these recipes so I always have the right amount on hand when a batch runs low.
